I’ve been struggling for a while now—maybe a couple of years, honestly. Ever since that incident on the flight back from Cancún—there was severe turbulence, screaming, oxygen masks dropping. I wasn’t hurt, but I couldn’t shake it afterward. Now, when I hear loud noises or someone even mentions flying, my chest gets tight, and my mind races back. I’ve started turning down work handling flight bookings, even though it’s part of my job. It’s easier to avoid it than to deal with that rush of fear.

I keep replaying it, wondering if I could’ve calmed people more, if I should’ve moved faster—I don’t know. I blame myself for freezing, even though logically, I know it wasn’t life-threatening. 

At the office, I sit facing the door, always aware of where the exits are. In restaurants, I can’t relax unless I’ve checked the room, noticed who’s around. It helps me feel a little safer. 

But I also have trouble focusing—on emails, on conversations—especially when I’m anxious. It’s not that I haven’t tried to pay attention, but things just slip. I don’t remember if this was always hard for me or if it started more recently. Either way, I’m falling behind, and I don’t know why exactly.
D018-D001_h019.question_a:
I’ve been feeling overwhelmed ever since that armed robbery at the travel agency two years ago. I was the only one in the office when it happened. I can’t go back to that building—even driving past it makes me break into a sweat, my chest tightens, and I start shaking. I’ve switched to working from home full time because I just can’t handle being in crowded or public spaces like I used to. I keep replaying it over and over—what I could’ve done differently. I should’ve hit the panic button faster. I blame myself for not protecting the company’s records, even though logically I know that doesn’t make sense.  

Now I’m always scanning the room, checking exits, watching everyone around me. At my daughter’s soccer games, instead of cheering, I’m analyzing people’s body language, wondering if someone seems “off.” And my focus—God, it’s gone. I used to juggle five bookings at once without missing a beat. Now I lose track mid-conversation, forget deadlines, can’t concentrate on emails. But it wasn’t like this before the robbery. I was focused, organized—especially as a single mom running things solo. The trouble with attention started after that day. It’s like my brain’s stuck in survival mode.

I blame myself, really. Sometimes a song or a place we used to go triggers this wave of guilt and sadness, and I have to leave, fast. I avoid those routes now, don’t even book trips to cities we visited together.  

But even outside of that, I’m scattered—miss details when clients explain their itineraries, forget appointments, lose paperwork. My mind’s always racing. And I catch myself scanning rooms, checking exits, watching people like I’m waiting for something bad to happen. But honestly? That’s nothing new either—I’ve always been this way, jumpy, unfocused. The trauma stuff feels layered on top, but the attention problems? Those were there since I was a child. I just thought I was lazy, or not trying hard enough.

I used to be able to focus, even under pressure, but now I can’t make it through a single chapter without my mind racing or collapsing into that hollow feeling again. I get panic attacks just walking past the building where it happened. I avoid that whole side of campus—I reroute my entire day to stay away.  

It’s like I’m always on edge, even in my apartment with the doors locked. I can’t relax. My shoulders are tight all the time, and I startle at noises most people don’t even notice. I keep thinking, *Why didn’t someone stop it? Why did they act like it wasn’t a big deal afterward?* It wasn’t just the attacker—I feel furious at people who knew and didn’t act, like they’re just as responsible.  

The worst part is my concentration. I used to be disciplined, but now I can’t hold a thought. I know this isn’t how I was before—it started after that night. Before age 12? No, I was a good student. This fog—it came with the memories.

I also get restless, like I can’t stay still during seminars—my legs bounce, I tap my pen, I just can’t settle.
